questions.title: Why did the court treat prior sightings of the same firearm as “intrinsic” rather than Rule 404(b) propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: Both D.F. and C.F. testified they had seen Cutbank with the sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle before the charged incident. The defense argued this was inadmissible propensity evidence under Rule 404(b), but the court deemed it intrinsic and cited United States v. Battle for the idea that prior possession of the same gun shows ownership/control. I'm confused about the Eighth Circuit’s test for when evidence is “intrinsic” (as opposed to a 404(b) other act). How is this not propensity reasoning, and what limiting principles are there? Also, even if intrinsic, is there still a Rule 403 balancing the court must conduct, and what would that look like here?

questions.title: When can officers repeat a victim’s statements “for context” without violating hearsay rules, and does later in-court testimony by the victim cure any Confrontation Clause problem?
questions.question_body: Pretrial, the defense asked for a limiting instruction so the jury wouldn’t consider D.F.’s statements to police as substantive evidence before she testified. The court declined to give an immediate instruction, the opinion says the trial did not admit hearsay, and notes the Confrontation Clause was satisfied because D.F. later testified. How do Eighth Circuit courts distinguish permissible "context" testimony (effect on listener) from impermissible hearsay where officers recount what a victim said? Is a contemporaneous limiting instruction ever required, or is a final instruction sufficient? If some officer testimony did slip into hearsay territory, does the victim’s later testimony eliminate any Confrontation Clause issue under cases like Crawford/Charboneau?

questions.title: How could the defense properly impeach C.F. using a police report she didn’t write?
questions.question_body: The defense tried to undermine C.F.’s “once or twice” prior-sighting testimony by reading portions of a police report. The court stopped counsel from reading the report into the record because C.F. did not author it and there was no proper authentication. Under FRE 613(b), what is the correct way to impeach a witness with a prior inconsistent statement memorialized in a third-party officer’s report? Do you need to call the officer to testify and authenticate the report, or get the witness to adopt the statement? Could FRE 803(5) (recorded recollection) or 612 (refreshing recollection) have been used? Why wasn’t reading the report aloud permissible as impeachment-only evidence?

questions.title: Was D.F.’s statement that her sister was killed by a gun properly admitted to explain inconsistencies, or should it have been excluded under Rule 403?
questions.question_body: On cross, D.F. explained some inconsistent statements by saying she was unfamiliar with and disliked guns "as [her] sister was killed by a gun." The defense moved to strike but the court denied, and later a similar reference came in through C.F. without objection. How do courts weigh the probative value of this kind of explanation for inconsistency or bias against the risk of unfair prejudice under Rule 403? Did the defense "open the door" by probing D.F.’s inconsistent statements, making this explanation fair response? Would a limiting instruction have been appropriate?

questions.title: What exactly qualified as the “other felony offense” for § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), and can the court rely on unobjected-to PSR facts to apply it?
questions.question_body: The PSR recommended a 4-level increase for possessing the firearm in connection with another felony, and the court adopted the PSR’s facts without objection. The opinion then says the court adopted "factual statements regarding [Cutbank’s] prior felony convictions" and "thus" found the gun was used in connection with another felony—this seems like a possible typo because prior convictions wouldn’t prove the nexus for the instant offense. Which felony was the "other" one here (e.g., kidnapping/false imprisonment, felony assault, terroristic threats, or resisting with injury)? What is the Eighth Circuit’s required nexus under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) (facilitated or had the potential to facilitate)? Is a preponderance standard applied, and is it proper to rely on unobjected-to PSR factual recitations alone to support the enhancement?

questions.title: Is base offense level 26 under § 2K2.1(a) correct for a sawed-off rifle plus two prior crimes of violence?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the PSR set a base offense level of 26 because the offense involved a § 5845(a) sawed-off firearm and Cutbank had at least two prior crimes of violence. I’m having trouble mapping that to the text of § 2K2.1(a) in the current Guidelines: some subsections hinge on the type of firearm (e.g., § 5845(a) firearms), others on number of prior crimes of violence or controlled substance offenses, and some combinations set different base levels (e.g., 22, 24, or 26). Which exact subsection(s) of § 2K2.1(a) in effect at the time support a 26 here, and why isn’t the correct base offense level 22 or 24 instead?

questions.title: Does applying § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) on top of ACCA, while also considering § 4B1.4’s “greater of” rule, risk impermissible double-counting?
questions.question_body: The panel notes the Armed Career Criminal Guideline (§ 4B1.4) would have yielded offense level 34, but the § 2K2.1 route with enhancements produced 35, so the greater applied. If the same conduct (possessing the gun "in connection with" another felony) could both trigger § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) and satisfy § 4B1.4(b)(3)(A)’s 34 level, is that double-counting? Or does the "use the greater of" directive resolve any double-counting concern because only the higher path is used? Is there Eighth Circuit authority squarely addressing this interaction?

questions.title: How does the Eighth Circuit’s presumption of reasonableness for within-Guidelines sentences interact with the § 3553(a) “not greater than necessary” principle?
questions.question_body: The court presumes a within-Guidelines sentence is reasonable (Goodhouse) and says a district court need not mechanically recite the § 3553(a) factors (Masood, Maluoth). If a defendant argues that guideline enhancements (e.g., § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), serial number, reckless endangerment) overstate the offense and that a lower sentence is “sufficient, but not greater than necessary,” what must the district court say to show it considered and rejected those arguments? On appeal, what kinds of arguments or record gaps are sufficient to overcome the presumption of reasonableness in the Eighth Circuit?
